title: Perfect Blue does not make any sense

commenti.body:
Satoshi Kohn is one of my alltime favorite directors, his passing broke my heart, I LOVE Perfect Blue...

  
... but I know better than to defend it's plot, holy shit. 

  
There is just no level of gaslighting that can induce those full on breaks from reality, those halucinations, and there is no way she did not commit at least one murder. Yeah, some are for sure the stalker, but I really feel like she was driven to kill at least once. 

I think the problem is that it was a trashy thriller elevated by Kohn which nobody expected to be a big deal, like some of the early Brian De Palma films which can be sleazy and incoherent but also... elevated and worth studying. I'm thinking Phantom of the Paradise, not even his 80s trashy thrillers. 

For sure check out Paranoia Agent if you have not... it is a better portrayal of anxiety and mental illness that builds to a head rather than serving as an excuse for full on flights of fancy... I mean you get insane flights of fancy but the characters and plot makes more sense.
who says it has to? we're talking about dream logic. you can say the same thing about a number of lynch films, it doesn't make them bad. they work on the level of sound and image, extraordinarily so.

What? The film is about a two women's psychological breakdown as they both lose their grip on their own identities. The idea that the camera is an objective observer is obviously played with, as the main theme of the movie is who we are vs how we are perceived.   
  
"I think it is a problem everybody has, male or female, famous or anonymous. I mean, there’s a gap between the image people see of me and what I see myself. *Perfect Blue* is about the tragedy caused by that gap becoming too large.”   
  
Sometimes it's the "real thing" sometimes it's a hallucination, just like in real life, it's not easy to discern which is which. Also, Rumi doesn't want to kill Mima at first. She's upset that Mima is leaving the idol life that Rumi so desperately wants back.  So, she tries to steer her back into her old career by increasingly violent means. She sees herself in Mima, and wants to "correct" her mistakes and live vicariously through here. This includes revenge on people who have hurt Mima along her new career path. This reaches a breaking point where she eventually dissociates enough to attempt to become Mima herself by killing her and subsuming her personality.

1. Because Mima has heard about the fact that these murders are occuring and has been gaslighted into believing  that she may be responsible but has no exact recollections if she did it or not. She's traumatized and tormented by all of these going around her so it makes complete sense that she would have this nightmare. Like you already see all those talking about it when she tries to get out of the apartment so yes, there is a way for her to know about them.

2. The police interrogations or questioning are possibly implied to be occuring through the meta scenes of the film where they are investigating fictional murders. It's also extremely unlikely from the police's perspective that she mightve committed these crimes given the fact that these attacks can be clearly inferred that they were committed by rabid fans. Not to mention that Mima seems be particularly busy with all of the work.

3. Sometimes, people who are victims of stalking and harrassmemt don't report to the police, especially given the fact that this kind of behavior has been particularly omnipresent in her career where people will send her questionable mails and ruin the concerts where she's in. Also, it makes sense with Mima's character. She's established as a young woman who is far too hesistant to speak her mind about her emotional problems and frustrationd but instead takes in all of that burden on herself due to guilt and because she feels pressured by everyone around her to dedicate to filling up her popular image over her mental health. Not to mention that as the narrative goes further, Mima is losing her mind from the escalation and cannot act rationally to call for real help, especially more later where she feels she may be the cause of these deaths.

4. Ok, so you admit it isn't really a plothole or issue at all? Police don't just catch serial killers immediately and it takes time and investigation? 

5. Again, like I said before, she feels that since it is in her room and that she's going mad, she might've murdered someone without remembering it. So if she were to show it to the police, they might really think she did it and put her in prison for it. Anyone would wanna avoid those consequences. Makes sense here.

6. What is being depicted here is "Folie á deux" or "Shared Psychotic Disorder", which is when multiple start believe and see the same illusions as if they were true. Kinda as if they were being transmitted to each other. It's an actual real thing and I think the use of the disorder in this film helps communicate one of the most fundamental messages of the film, which is about how social pressure and cultural norms reinforce ideas about how people should feel about themselves according to how they're being perceived by the public. It works to represent the "psychosis" of how Japanese men see young women through a very narrow and oppressive role and how those toxic beliefs can also become part of the mindest of the person going through the pressures. In this case, Mima having to be the infantilized idea of femininity that is a pop idol (which has gone through real-life critique for such things like harsh work conditions, limiting the freedom of what their female celebrities can do in their personal lives and also how they sometimes hired underage girls who inevitably got them sexualized) and also that when she moves on to more adult roles, it represents for the public a kind of "deflorization" of her pure image, causing the slut shaming and further dehumanization of Mima. This also affects Rumi because she was also herself a pop idol and very likely went through much of the same social pressures as Mima (probably because of her weight and age since pop idols are meant to go through very unrealistic standards of beauty and fitness), which further explains why in part they have such commonality in sharing that psychosis. And as the other person has said, this is about two women losing their sense of reality, which causes the camera to look at events through a very subjective perspective which makes facts and fiction ambiguous. And that even in less extreme cases, we at times see and hear things that aren't there and these pressures further amplify those moments of delusion.

7. As the other commenter has said, Rumi did not want to kill Mima at first and was trying to save the ideal that she perceived about her but we slowly see her descend more and more into complete madness as this fantasy is destroyed for her. We start noticing this when Mima performs the rape scene. Rumi is clearly devastated by this ane it's what pushes her further to kill those people. She starts blaming the men for taking away the "real" Mima but then eventually pushes that blame onto Mima herself for "betraying" that image for one in adult movies. So she takes means by her own hands and believes dtrongly that she should hold on to the identity, which is a false one being held by someone who isn't even the originator of the title. 

8. Ummmmm, yes, they do fit and I explained them very well. You just need to pay attention and understand that the movie very purposefully plays around with reality and fiction to put us in the perspective of thr protagonist herself, who is losing her grip in reality and sees things that seem inconsistent and wrong. Not everything is a delusion but delusions combining themselves with reality. Like the other commenter has said, it's working through a type of dream logic. Not literally all a dream but presenting how sometimes the fallacious human mind can view the world around them. Just because you haven't noticed it doesn't mean there isn't a reasonably answer for why the film show these events in the way they do.

9. And it isn't random. It's very deliberately meant to be mindbending, off-putting and ambiguous to reinforce its themes of psychosis and hoe reality and fiction can become blurred due to real external forces influencing those ideas.
